paragraphs.heading: Life where little was expected
paragraphs.text: A deep-sea community is any community of organisms tied to a shared habitat in the deep sea. These communities remain largely unexplored, because visiting this remote biome is technically and logistically hard and expensive. The deep sea poses unique challenges, particularly high pressure, extremes of temperature and no light. For a long time people believed little life existed in so hostile a place. Since the 19th century, though, research has shown that the deep sea holds significant biodiversity.

paragraphs.heading: Layers of light
paragraphs.text: The ocean can be pictured as divided into zones, according to depth and whether sunlight is present. The photic zone is the layer of water down to which sunlight penetrates. Its uppermost part, the euphotic zone, has enough light for phytoplankton and plants to carry out photosynthesis. Its lower part, the dysphotic zone or twilight zone, has too little light for photosynthesis and reaches down to about 1000 meters. Below the photic zone, all the way to the seabed, lies the aphotic zone, a region of perpetual darkness.

paragraphs.heading: Why sunlight matters
paragraphs.text: Nearly all life forms in the ocean depend on phytoplankton and other marine plants, whose photosynthesis turns carbon dioxide into organic carbon, the basic building block of organic matter. Photosynthesis needs energy from sunlight. The ocean's average depth is about 3688 meters, so the photic zone is only a tiny fraction of its total volume. Yet of all oceanic zones the photic zone has the greatest biodiversity and biomass, and nearly all primary production in the ocean happens there.

paragraphs.heading: Finding food in the dark
paragraphs.text: Any life in the aphotic zone has three options. It must be able to move up through the water into the photic zone to feed, or rely on material sinking from above, or find another source of energy and nutrition. Chemosynthetic archaea found near hydrothermal vents and cold seeps are an example of the last. Deep sea communities draw their energy and nutrients from three main sources: chemosynthesis at hydrothermal vents and cold seeps, whale falls, and marine snow.

paragraphs.heading: Built for pressure
paragraphs.text: Deep-sea animals have evolved to survive the extreme pressure below the photic zone. Pressure rises by about one atmosphere every ten meters. To cope, many fish are rather small, usually no longer than 25 cm. Scientists have also found that creatures living deeper have more gelatinous flesh and a more minimal skeleton.

paragraphs.heading: Going down to look
paragraphs.text: In the 1870s Sir Charles Wyville Thomson and colleagues on the Challenger expedition found many deep-sea creatures, of widely varying types. In 1960 Don Walsh and Jacques Piccard went down to the bottom of the Challenger Deep, the deepest surveyed point in all of Earth's oceans, in the bathyscaphe Trieste. At that depth a small flounder-like fish was seen as it moved away from the craft's spotlight. A deep-sea chemosynthetic community that included higher animals was first discovered, unexpectedly, during geological explorations, at hydrothermal vents in the eastern Pacific Ocean.
